steps.title: In the ground

form.name: Ore
form.label: a few grams in every tonne

steps.text: The six platinum-group metals occur together. Most lie in a few thin layers of the Bushveld Complex in South Africa, an ancient body of once-molten rock, with more in Zimbabwe's Great Dyke. In Russia and Canada they come as a by-product of nickel and copper sulphide ore. Ruthenium is a minor part of the mix, richest in South Africa's UG2 reef.

steps.title: Mine
steps.text: The South African reefs are about a metre thick and are followed more than a kilometre underground. Miners drill and blast the narrow seam and haul the rock to the shaft. It is deep, hot and labour-intensive work.

steps.title: Concentrate
steps.text: The ore is milled to powder and floated. The platinum-group metals follow the nickel and copper sulphide grains into a concentrate that is a small fraction of the rock mined.

steps.title: Smelt
steps.text: An electric furnace melts the concentrate. Silicates leave as slag and the metals collect in a matte of nickel, copper and iron sulphide. A converter burns off the iron. The nickel and copper are then leached away for sale, leaving a residue rich in precious metals.

steps.title: Refine
steps.text: The residue is dissolved in hydrochloric acid and chlorine. One by one the metals are pulled out by solvent extraction, precipitation and distillation, in a refinery where material can spend weeks or months. Ruthenium is one of the minor metals. It is distilled off as a volatile oxide and captured.

steps.title: Make
steps.text: Ruthenium powder is pressed into sputtering targets, made into pastes for chip resistors, or loaded onto supports as a catalyst.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: A layer of ruthenium a few atoms thick sits in every hard-disk platter. Ruthenium oxide paste makes the resistors on circuit boards, and ruthenium-coated anodes make chlorine. It is a candidate for wiring in the most advanced chips.
steps.india: All imported, for electronics and chemicals.

steps.title: Recycle
steps.text: Spent sputtering targets and catalysts go back to the refiner. Ruthenium in consumer electronics is too thinly spread to recover.
steps.india: Hindustan Platinum and other refiners recover platinum-group metals from spent catalysts. A Rs 1,500 crore recycling scheme (2025) covers catalytic converters.
